{{Notability|date=March 2024}}
{{one source |date=May 2024}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''[[tensor product]] of [[quadratic form]]s''' is most easily understood when one views the quadratic forms as ''[[quadratic space]]s''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kitaoka |first1=Yoshiyuki |title=Tensor products of positive definite quadratic forms IV |journal=Nagoya Mathematical Journal |date=1979 |volume=73 |pages=149–156 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/nagoya-mathematical-journal/article/tensor-products-of-positive-definite-quadratic-forms-iv/1F360E61EDA5EBAA4C86C64F987C82D1 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/S0027763000018365 |access-date=February 12, 2024}}</ref> If ''R'' is a [[commutative ring]] where 2 is [[Unit (ring theory)|invertible]], and if <math>(V_1, q_1)</math> and <math>(V_2,q_2)</math> are two quadratic spaces over ''R'', then their tensor product <math>(V_1 \otimes V_2, q_1 \otimes q_2)</math> is the quadratic space whose underlying ''R''-[[Module (mathematics)|module]] is the [[Tensor product of modules|tensor product]] <math>V_1 \otimes V_2</math> of ''R''-modules and whose quadratic form is the quadratic form associated to the tensor product of the [[bilinear form]]s associated to <math>q_1</math> and <math>q_2</math>.

In particular, the form <math>q_1 \otimes q_2</math> satisfies

:<math> (q_1\otimes q_2)(v_1 \otimes v_2) = q_1(v_1) q_2(v_2) \quad \forall v_1 \in V_1,\ v_2 \in V_2</math>

(which does uniquely characterize it however). It follows from this that if the quadratic forms are diagonalizable (which is always possible if 2 is invertible in ''R''), i.e., 

:<math>q_1 \cong \langle a_1, ... , a_n \rangle</math>
:<math>q_2 \cong \langle b_1, ... , b_m \rangle</math>

then the tensor product has diagonalization

:<math>q_1 \otimes q_2 \cong \langle a_1b_1, a_1b_2, ... a_1b_m, a_2b_1, ... , a_2b_m , ... , a_nb_1, ... a_nb_m \rangle.</math>
